newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks sell off, hit by bonds and oil worries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks sell off, hit by bonds and oil worries.

text.p: U.S. stocks were hit by a late wave of heavy selling pressure on Thursday amid a sell-off in bonds and concerns that higher oil prices might fuel inflation and push interest rates higher.

Stocks, which spent the day swinging from negative to positive ground, took a sharp downturn after news that Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries reached a pact to limit overproduction, which has kept a lid on oil prices.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 68.08, or 0.88 percent, unofficially to 7689.98 in very heavy trading.

Analysts said the financial markets were also spooked by rumors that a foreign central bank may have been the party that unloaded $1.0 billion of 10-year Treasury notes during the day. That sent the bond market reeling.
The yield on the benchmark 30-year government bond was pushed to 6.74 percent as the price fell 20/32.

"The market is very nervous. The Dow traveled 450 points back and forth today with nothing concrete. There were rumors of foreigners selling in bonds and crude rose slightly after OPEC," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

Analysts said comments made by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin did nothing to calm the markets. U.S. markets were rocked Monday after a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that sparked fears Japan might sell some of its large holdings of U.S. government bonds.
On Wednesday, Rubin said there was no reason to expect such sales and the market could absorb them if they occurred.
"Why would he say that except to possibly cushion a blow? Market players are very skeptical about remarks like that," one analyst said.
In stocks, the trading day brought a rollercoaster ride of wide swings that mirrored smaller movements in bonds. Trading has been volatile and volume heavy all week.

Early in the session, the Dow fell about 50 points, then reversed course and climbed to a gain of 50 points before the sharp sell-off. At its nadir, the average was off almost 130 points before backtracking to its closing level.

"The recent volatility is due to the increasing skittishness of market participants. It's normally not a very good thing. But it tends to happen around highs and lows," said Harry Laubscher, market analyst at Tucker Anthony.
The August crude oil futures contract closed up 49 cents at $19.52 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Oil stocks fell, with Exxon Corp down 1-9/16 at 60-15/16 and Chevron Corp off 7/16 at 73-13/16. The Standard & Poor's Oil Index .SPOIL dropped 12 points to 1371.

Almost all of the 30 Dow components closed lower, with only Sears Roebuck and Co, Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co and AT&T Corp ekeing out gains. AT&T rose 1/16 to 37 amid broad strength in telecom stocks.
Gold-mining stocks also prospered as inflation tensions grew. The S&P Gold Index rose two percent to 195.3 points.

Among individual issues, Liposome Co Inc's share price dropped 60 percent after the company said its lead respiratory drug, Ventus, did no better than a placebo in a Phase III clinical trial. The drug had shown no such weakness in earlier tests. The stock closed down 15-4/16 to 9-9/16.

Some small stocks were punished after issuing profit warnings. Gadzooks Inc, which makes fashion clothing for teen-agers, sunk 15-1/2 to 20-1/8 after it said second-quarter sales and earnings would disappoint.
3Com Corp fell 1-3/8 to 48-3/8. The company said late Tuesday it expected its revenue growth to slow.
Decliners beat advancers 1,558 to 1,254 on volume of 603.0 million shares, according to the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said volume has high all week as money managers scramble to square away their portfolios ahead of the official end of the quarter on June 30.
The S&P 500 closed down 7.35 to 888.99.
The Nasdaq Composite closed down 6.19 to 1446.24.
((Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1881))
